title: perf: Use full-rate FADD relu in SM90 FP8 MQA logits epilogue by Chtholly-Boss · Pull Request #452 · deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM · GitHub
body:

Summary
Replace
fmaxf(x, 0)
with
x + fabsf(x)
in the SM90 FP8 MQA logits epilogue, recovering the 2× throughput gap between FMNMX (half-rate) and FADD (full-rate) on Hopper. The factor-of-2 introduced by the identity is resolved by folding
0.5f
into the existing
scale_kv
multiply — zero extra instructions, bit-exact numerics.
Background
On SM90,
fmaxf(x, 0)
compiles to a single FMNMX, which issues at 64 ops/clk/SM — half the rate of FADD/FFMA (128 ops/clk/SM). Meanwhile
x + |x|
compiles to a single FADD with the absolute-value operand modifier, which is a free encoding bit in the instruction word:
FADD R3, R3, |R3|    ; one instruction, full rate (cuobjdump, sm_90a)
The relu executes once per
(token, head, kv)
score element in the MQA logits epilogue, so at 64 vs 128 ops/clk/SM the FMNMX form doubles the FP32 pipe time spent on relu alone.
Since
x + |x| = 2 · relu(x)
holds exactly for all finite IEEE-754 floats (
+0
for x ≤ 0), the doubled sum is simply halved by folding
* 0.5f
into the already-existing
scale_kv
multiplication (an exponent decrement, also exact):
//
Before:
return
fmaxf(shifted_accum[j],
0
) * weights[i][(j /
4
) *
2
+ (j &
1
)];

0
] + sum[
1
]) * scale_kv_0;
//
After:
return
(shifted_accum[j] + fabsf(shifted_accum[j])) * weights[i][(j /
4

+ (j &

...

The same technique is already used by the SM100 kernel (
sm100_mqa_logits.cuh
, packed
FADD2
variant); this PR brings it to SM90. Verified via
cuobjdump -sass
: zero FMNMX across all JIT-instantiated
sm90_fp8_mqa_logits
cubins.
Performance (H200, 132 SMs, SM90A)

Full
tests/test_attention.py
sweep (192 contiguous MQA cases on SM90):
avg +3.7%
(SK=65536 subset +4.4%, H=64 subset +5.5%, best case +11.3%). Gains scale with the relu's share of kernel time: larger SKV, more heads, smaller head dim → bigger win. Paged MQA logits (separate kernel, untouched) is unaffected.
Correctness
x + |x| = 2 · relu(x)
exactly for all finite IEEE-754 floats (x > 0:
x + x = 2x
; x ≤ 0:
x + (−x) = +0
); the ÷2 via
* 0.5f
is an exact exponent decrement.
All 192 SM90 cases in
tests/test_attention.py
pass (numeric diff vs simulated reference, 20× bitwise self-consistency, mask equality) — verified on H200.
NaN semantics differ (
x + |x|
propagates NaN;
fmaxf(NaN, 0)
returns 0), but WGMMA accumulator outputs are finite in practice; this matches the SM100 kernel's existing behavior.
Changes
deep_gemm/include/deep_gemm/impls/sm90_fp8_mqa_logits.cuh
— 3 lines modified (transform lambda + two
* 0.5f
folds).

v6
已核对完整 epilogue、调用约束及 SM100 既有实现，未发现需要修复的回归；ReLU 倍增与两路缩放补偿一致。当前环境没有 CUDA 工具链或 GPU，未复跑测试或验证性能。
v5
LGTM — approve.
The MR replaces
fmaxf(x, 0)
with
x + fabsf(x)
in the SM90 FP8 MQA logits epilogue (
sm90_fp8_mqa_logits.cuh
) and folds the compensating
* 0.5f
into the existing per-KV
scale_kv
multiply. The diff is exactly 3 lines and matches the description.
Verified points:
Numerics:
x + |x| == 2*relu(x)
is exact for all finite IEEE-754 floats (x>0: 2x; x<=0: exactly +0).
scale_kv * 0.5f
is an exact exponent decrement. Result is bit-identical to the previous path for finite accumulators.
Placement of the
0.5f
fold is correct: applied once per output element after the intra-thread reduction
(sum[0]+sum[1])
/
(sum[2]+sum[3])
and before the
__shfl_xor_sync
inter-thread reduction, so each of the
kNumHeads
contributing terms is halved exactly once.
scale_kv_0/1
are loop-invariant across the
BLOCK_Q
loop, so
scale_kv * 0.5f
is hoisted by nvcc — genuinely zero extra instructions per element.
NaN semantics:
fmaxf(NaN, 0)
returned 0, whereas
NaN + |NaN|
propagates NaN. This matches the SM100 kernel (
sm100_mqa_logits.cuh
L492-506 already uses the identical
x + |x|
trick via
__fadd2_rn
followed by
/ 2
), and WGMMA FP8 accumulators are finite in practice, so this is acceptable and consistent rather than new risk.
Scope: the paged MQA logits kernel is untouched, as stated.
No blocking issues. Performance claims (+3.7% avg, +7.4% on production shape, zero FMNMX in SASS) are plausible given FMNMX is half-rate on SM90 and the abs operand modifier is a free encoding bit on FADD; they were not re-measured here (no Hopper GPU in this environment). Two non-blocking, purely maintainability-oriented suggestions are left inline.
v4
Correct, low-risk SM90 micro-optimization. The MR replaces the half-rate
fmaxf(x, 0)
ReLU in the SM90 FP8 MQA logits epilogue with a full-rate FADD using the free absolute-value operand modifier (
x + |x|
), and compensates the resulting exact factor of 2 by folding
* 0.5f
into the already-present
scale_kv
multiply. I verified the change end to end: (1) for every finite IEEE-754 float,
x + |x| == 2*relu(x)
exactly (+0 for x <= 0, and
x + x == 2x
exactly for x > 0); (2) the factor-of-2 is uniform across the per-term weight multiply and across both the intra-thread and inter-thread (shuffle-xor) reductions, so it factors out exactly; (3)
scale_kv * 0.5f
is an exact power-of-two scaling for normal scales, so
fl((2*sum) * (scale/2)) == fl(sum * scale)
is bit-exact versus the previous
fmaxf
path. The change is local (3 lines in one file: line 286 transform plus the two
* 0.5f
folds at lines 297-298), preserves the kernel's dataflow/synchronization, and is consistent with the existing SM100
sm100_mqa_logits.cuh
implementation that already uses the same
fabsf
+
/2
identity. The claimed SASS result (a single FADD with the abs operand modifier replacing FMNMX) is consistent with the documented SM90 issue rates. Verified caveats, none blocking: (a) only non-finite inputs differ, since
fmaxf(NaN, 0) == 0
while
x + |x|
propagates NaN and
x == -inf
gives
NaN
; WGMMA accumulator outputs are finite in practice and this matches the SM100 kernel, so it is acceptable; (b) the exactness of the halving relies on
scale_kv
being normal (subnormal halving could lose a bit, and the doubled accumulator could overflow only near FLT_MAX), which realistic FP8 dequant scales and attention logits never approach. No correctness, safety, API, or concurrency issues found, and no changes requested.

Add H200 TP8 DSv4.1 Flash AgentX at concurrency 1–128, using the full
semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126
corpus. Five-token DSpark throughput uses
golden AL 3.51
(thinking on), with adaptive verification disabled; accuracy evals retain real block verification. Engram stays in host DRAM through UVA; KV stays on GPU. Validation: Bash, exact-key matrix, changelog, launcher/eval tests, and both serving-mode command checks pass. GPU validation pending.
新增 H200 TP8 DSv4.1 Flash AgentX，并发 1–128，使用完整
semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126
语料。五 token DSpark 吞吐测试采用 thinking 开启时的黄金 AL 3.51，并关闭自适应验证；准确率 eval 保留真实块验证。Engram 通过 UVA 访问主机 DRAM，KV 保留在 GPU。验证：Bash、精确配置矩阵、changelog、launcher/eval 测试及两种服务模式的命令检查通过；GPU 验证待完成。
Note
Medium Risk
New cluster benchmark recipe and Slurm launcher behavior for a model prefix, plus shared port-selection helper used at serve time; GPU validation is still pending.
Overview
Adds
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
(
dsv41flash
) to the model matrix and introduces the
H200 TP8 AgentX
recipe
dsv41flash-fp4-h200-vllm-agentic-dspark
in
nvidia-master.yaml
, with perf-changelog and EN/zh configuration docs (including rationale for no H100 arm).
The new vLLM agentic launcher serves
1M context
with
Engram CPU UVA offload
,
GPU-resident KV
,
five-token DSpark
(throughput pins golden AL
3.51
; eval keeps real verification), and replays the
uncapped
semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126
corpus via the existing
dsv4*
trace default.
Infrastructure:
select_available_server_port()
in
benchmark_lib.sh
avoids host-network port collisions; H200 Slurm launcher mounts the repo at
/ix
for
dsv41flash
so AgentX runtime dirs stay out of
/workspace
. Tests cover launcher mounts, trace corpus selection, and port probing.

* config(dsv41flash): change the MI355X memory split only where KV ran short

The previous commit applied one memory split per TP across every
concurrency. Concurrency 1-32 never ran short of KV, so it paid for
changes it did not need: offloaded Engram lookups go to pinned host
memory over UVA, and a smaller prefill chunk costs TTFT. Scope each
change to the points that were actually starved, which also leaves
concurrency 1-32 and TP=4 c64 byte-identical to the settings run
35574132719 already measured on this image and flag set, so those
points are combined with this sweep rather than re-run.

Dividing measured KV tokens by concurrency gives the per-request budget
and separates the failures cleanly. Every point that held had 232K or
more; TP=2 c64 collapsed at 122K.

  TP=4 c1-c64   resident, 16384   14.83M tokens   232K and up
  TP=4 c128     offload,   8192   49.63M           388K
  TP=2 c1-c32   offload,  16384    7.84M           245K and up
  TP=2 c64      offload,   8192   24.68M           386K
  TP=2 c128     offload,   4096   33.34M           260K

Probing the configurations directly also turned up two things. TP=2 c128
at 4096 with the API-server default of 1024 sequences faults during
profiling with HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION at M=1024, N=129280, K=256,
reproduced on two GPU pairs: DSpark verifies 1+5 tokens per sequence, so
a decode batch of max_num_seqs needs six times that many token slots and
4096 leaves four. Cap max_num_seqs at the graph-capture shape wherever
the chunk falls below that bound, which is TP=2 c128 alone. And the
reason c128 never completed before is that at 16384 with capture at
2048, TP=2 c128 held 7.72 GiB, 3.02M tokens, 23.6K per request.

* refactor(minimaxm3-atom): one table per concurrency, and drop the tier M3 cannot use

The hybrid offload tier is unreachable for this model. ATOM's M3 connector is
PAGE-only -- the docstring says MiniMax-M3 has no recurrent state and no SLOT
sidecar, and it raises if slot_regions is non-empty -- so OFFLOAD_STATE and the
staging knobs behind STATE_OFFLOAD_CPU_GIB never applied. Its LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE
is justified by "block-size(128) x dcp(8)", but this model's search space sets
no dcp-size at all. Removed, along with the comment claiming M3 carries a
per-request recurrent state. An unlisted concurrency now fails instead of
silently taking a tier that does not fit.

CONC=56 is removed for the same reason: nothing in the matrix runs it here (the
56 in this file's neighbourhood belongs to Kimi K3, which has its own script),
and it was the only band that disabled the draft model. With it gone
NUM_SPEC_TOKENS is constant, so the guard around SPEC_ARGS goes too.

The remaining per-concurrency facts now live in one table. Previously the CP
gate was a numeric comparison and the offload tier an enumeration, so adding a
concurrency above 24 would silently enable indexer CP on a point nobody
measured, while forgetting the tier failed loudly. Both are declared per band
now: the loud failure is kept, the silent one becomes a missing speedup.

Verified the same way as the previous cleanup: all 19 matrix points replayed
through a stubbed benchmark_lib, server argv and every exported env var
byte-identical.

* perf(minimaxm3-atom): extend indexer CP down to CONC=15 on TP4

The gate was CONC > 24, chosen from a kernel microbenchmark over uniform
contexts. Three same-commit A/B pairs (1800 s per arm, TP4 + EAGLE3) put the
real crossover below 15:

  CONC 15   interactivity p90 +3.7%    ISL-normalised throughput +0.67%
  CONC 24                    +12.3%                              +0.24%
  CONC 28                    +16.7%                              +2.7%

Monotone and never negative. Throughput is neutral everywhere (only CONC=28
clears the 0.6% noise floor) while interactivity rises with the running batch,
which is what CP actually shortens. Prefix hit rates are identical within each
pair (96.7/96.7, 97.5/97.5, 97.2/97.3), so the gain is not a caching artifact.

CONC=20 is interpolated between the two measured points, not run on its own.
Nothing below 15 is measured and the microbenchmark is negative at batch ~2,
so the band stops there.

CONC=20 appears in both search-space rows, so it is split out of the offload
enumeration: TP4 gets CP without a tier, and the tp_size == 4 gate keeps CP off
the TP2 offload curve. 25 and 30 are TP2-only and stay without a CP
declaration, which would never take effect but would misreport the point.

Verified with the 19-point argv+env replay: the only difference against the
previous revision is ATOM_M3_INDEXER_CP="1" on tp4_c15, tp4_c20 and tp4_c24.

* config(dsv41flash): disable SWA bounded replay on MI355X

Every TP=2 and TP=4 point of run 35567570539 died with
HSA_STATUS_ERROR_MEMORY_FAULT, taking the worker and then the engine core
down and aborting AgentX warmup. The fault follows the first launch of
_pad_replayed_slots_kernel in all 16 server logs, which is the first
prefix hit carrying a replay start.

vllm-project/vllm#56227 added SWA bounded replay, default on, after the
eed1f3d0 pin and before nightly-rocm100-3df4ae153. It pads the replayed
tokens' slots in the prefix-cacheable groups, but the window clamp it
relies on landed in the FlashInfer and FlashMLA kernels; the ROCm sparse
SWA path only gained the replay_start kwarg, and consumes it on the
decode path while the fault is in prefill. Pass --no-swa-bounded-replay
until ROCm clamps too. Prefix caching itself stays on.

运行 35567570539 的所有 TP=2 与 TP=4 数据点都以
HSA_STATUS_ERROR_MEMORY_FAULT 崩溃，先后带崩 worker 与 engine core，
并中止 AgentX warmup。16 份 server 日志中，该故障均紧随
_pad_replayed_slots_kernel 的首次启动，即首个带 replay start 的前缀命中。

引入了默认开启的 SWA bounded replay。它会填充被重放 token 在可前缀缓存
分组中的 slot，但其依赖的窗口钳制只落在 FlashInfer 与 FlashMLA 内核中；
ROCm 稀疏 SWA 路径仅新增了 replay_start 参数，且只在 decode 路径消费它，
而故障发生在 prefill。在 ROCm 同样实现钳制之前传入
--no-swa-bounded-replay。前缀缓存本身保持开启。

* config(dsv41flash): fix the MI355X KV split at high concurrency

Concurrency 64 collapsed on both arms of run 35574132719 because the KV
pool was too small to hold the AgentX working set. TP=2 fell to a 17.6%
prefix cache hit rate, 187 s TTFT and 150 tok/s, against 94.8%, 1.3 s and
957 tok/s at c32.

Two settings were spending device memory that the KV pool needed.

The Engram tables stayed resident at TP=4. vllm-project/vllm#57491
widened the two ROCm is_cuda() gates to is_cuda_alike(), so gfx950 can
now offload them to pinned host memory as every NVIDIA arm has since
 #2963. Measured here at TP=4 with 16384 batched tokens, resident tables
leave 37.96 GiB of KV cache and 14.15x maximum concurrency at 1M
context, against 84.54 GiB and 31.52x offloaded.

The sparse-attention indexer and its companion per-rank buffers scale at
roughly 4.4 MiB per batched token, so the upstream 16384 was the larger
cost. Size it per TP instead, 4096 at TP=2 and 8192 at TP=4, and cap
max_num_seqs at the shape graph capture already covers rather than the
MI355X API-server default of 1024. TP=2 then keeps 79.34 GiB (39.44x)
and TP=4 keeps 121.03 GiB (54.15x), against the B300 arm's 132.48 GiB
(60.17x). B300 runs 8192 at TP=4 and the Blackwell TP=2 arms run 4096
(#3320, #3321).

Sweep concurrency 64 and 128 to confirm the high end first. Concurrency
1-32 is backfilled once those land, since every point now runs the new
memory split.

Co-authored-by: Cursor Agent <cursoragent@cursor.com>
Signed-off-by: Fangzhou Ai <fangzhou.ai@amd.com>

* config(dsv41flash): change the MI355X memory split only where KV ran short

The previous commit applied one memory split per TP across every
concurrency. Concurrency 1-32 never ran short of KV, so it paid for
changes it did not need: offloaded Engram lookups go to pinned host
memory over UVA, and a smaller prefill chunk costs TTFT. Scope each
change to the points that were actually starved, which also leaves
concurrency 1-32 and TP=4 c64 byte-identical to the settings run
35574132719 already measured on this image and flag set, so those
points are combined with this sweep rather than re-run.

Dividing measured KV tokens by concurrency gives the per-request budget
and separates the failures cleanly. Every point that held had 232K or
more; TP=2 c64 collapsed at 122K.

  TP=4 c1-c64   resident, 16384   14.83M tokens   232K and up
  TP=4 c128     offload,   8192   49.63M           388K
  TP=2 c1-c32   offload,  16384    7.84M           245K and up
  TP=2 c64      offload,   8192   24.68M           386K
  TP=2 c128     offload,   4096   33.34M           260K

Probing the configurations directly also turned up two things. TP=2 c128
at 4096 with the API-server default of 1024 sequences faults during
profiling with HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION at M=1024, N=129280, K=256,
reproduced on two GPU pairs: DSpark verifies 1+5 tokens per sequence, so
a decode batch of max_num_seqs needs six times that many token slots and
4096 leaves four. Cap max_num_seqs at the graph-capture shape wherever
the chunk falls below that bound, which is TP=2 c128 alone. And the
reason c128 never completed before is that at 16384 with capture at
2048, TP=2 c128 held 7.72 GiB, 3.02M tokens, 23.6K per request.

title: Add opt-in borrowed receive storage for compact BF16 dispatch
body:
`dispatch(..., borrow_recv=True)` skips the activation copy of the dispatch epilogue: the epilogue writes only metadata plus a row map and returns a `DispatchRecvView` (`slab`, `row_indices`) over the communication buffer, which an indexed consumer such as a gathered GEMM reads directly. The view holds an exclusive lease: `release(*streams)` orders the next communication after the consumers, and dispatch/combine/LB calls/`destroy()` reject an active view. Supported: fresh compact BF16 dispatch within one NVLink domain with CPU counts and `defer_epilogue=False`; everything else is rejected up front. Default behavior is unchanged.

8×H200, deterministic, hidden 3072, top-8, 16 local experts, dispatch plus the same indexed consumer: −13.1% at 8192 tokens/rank and −13.5% at 16384, but +15.9% at 1024, hence opt-in. Fixed-route serial forward only; no overlap or training-throughput claim. Combined with DeepGEMM #463 in a live EP8 + gate/up GEMM + SwiGLU step: −17%. Raw cycles and the reproducer: [gist](https://gist.github.com/yuweih205/d3fd1e4c3fcb97364f36ec8fda996cfe).

Test: `python tests/ep/test_recv_view.py --num-processes 8` (bitwise payload/metadata against the gathered inputs, replay/combine after release, delayed cross-stream readers, invalid-mode rejection).

Re-validated 2026-10-16 at 71157be (100350f differs only in documentation; native code byte-identical to the measured build) on 8×H200, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu132: `test_recv_view.py` 16/16 cases under both `EP_AVOID_RECORD_STREAM` policies; the EP8 functional suite passes with CPU counts for direct and deferred epilogues. With `--do-cpu-sync 0` the unmodified suite stops at its full-capacity `recv_x_twice` comparison on this branch exactly as on upstream main; with the valid-prefix comparison from #786 it passes on both.

title: Fix cross-stream waits after deferred epilogues
body:
## Summary

Retain a completion event after a successfully executed `EventOverlap` hook, so
later waits on other CUDA streams also depend on the work enqueued by that hook.

The event returned by the communication operation precedes its deferred epilogue.
The first wait runs the hook on its current stream and clears the hook; another
stream currently waits only for the original communication event. It can then
read tensors before the epilogue's GPU work is complete. The same issue applies
to deterministic sorting registered as an after-wait hook.

The fix keeps the original event and its retained tensors alive, records a
separate native `EventHandle` after the hook succeeds, and includes it in later
waits. Explicit `release_handle=True` releases both event handles. Hooks still
run once and only the first wait returns their result. A failing hook remains
retryable. The ordinary no-hook path records no additional CUDA event. No
host/device synchronization is added.

## Regression coverage

The current diff includes a standalone two-function CUDA regression in
`tests/utils/test_event.py`:

- A deliberately delayed hook writer and a second-stream reader, with a raw
  original-event negative control, repeated waits, single-hook execution and
  explicit event-handle release. The test requires the delayed write to still
  be pending when the negative control completes; an ineffective window fails.
- A no-hook wait and context-manager release, checking that no extra epilogue
  event is recorded.

Run it in an installed/built checkout:

```bash
python tests/utils/test_event.py
```

### Historical extended harness

The earlier standalone CUDA regression harness, retained in the tested commit
[`e15813d`](https://github.com/yuweih205/DeepEP/blob/e15813df91be6a4288b280b8cb26a5e84b96c0e0/tests/utils/test_event.py), checks:

- Two subsequent reader streams after a deliberately delayed writer hook,
  with and without explicit release.
- Context-manager waits after a prior hook on a different stream.
- Multi-stream CUDA Graph capture and three replays.
- No extra event capture when no hook is registered.
- Hook failure/retry and first-wait return semantics.

Its eager race tests require the delayed write to still be pending before the
reader is queued. Otherwise they fail as an ineffective race test. They drain
both streams even if an assertion fails. This historical five-method harness
is not the current two-function regression.

## Validation

### Current polished revision

Head: `ebaaab5f4b58d3fd96ccbc9ba66481ba41cd1703`, based on public main
`b5a33eefda39485f438dc764695b71ba7b9249b6`.

Both current CUDA regression functions passed on H200 with PyTorch
`2.13.0+cu132`, CUDA 13.2 and NCCL 2.32.3. This run covers the current
two-function regression, not a rerun of the extended historical harness or
its CUDA Graph cases. The production wrapper's Python AST matches the
previously published fixed implementation.

### Historical extended validation

Validated on eight H200 141GB GPUs, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu132, CUDA 13.2 and NCCL
2.32.3. Base: public main `93eb6eb238127e96c6d7a4a625a6dad158348509`; pinned
DeepJIT `cba802df081985141eeee36803685775c183a047`. The `_C` extension was built
from those unmodified native sources. Only the Python event wrapper differs
between the original/fixed regression arms.

- Original wrapper: all 24 suites (three per GPU) reproduce stale reads in
  both explicit-reader release cases and the context-manager case. The CUDA
  Graph case also reproduces stale reads in all 24 suites.
- Fixed wrapper: all 24 suites pass all five methods (120 method runs), with
  no skipped tests. Each Graph test verifies three replays.
- Upstream EP8 functional suite, deterministic, CPU counts enabled: all 36
  deferred-epilogue configurations and all 72 non-deferred configurations pass.
  This covers fresh/cached, compact/expanded, BF16/FP8 dispatch and combine,
  bias variants, previous-event and allocation-stream settings, and repeated
  deterministic dispatch checks.

These results belong to the earlier extended harness and functional-suite
validation. That larger harness is not included in the current diff; the
two-function CUDA regression above is included.

Re-run the upstream EP8 functional suite in an installed/built checkout:

```bash
for deferred in 1 0; do
    python tests/ep/test_ep.py --num-processes 8 --num-tokens 128 --hidden 512 \
        --num-topk 2 --num-experts 16 --num-sms 8 --skip-perf-test \
        --deterministic --defer-epilogue "$deferred"
done
```

The first historical build attempt stopped before tests because the image
lacked the DeepJIT dependency `elfutils/libdwfl.h`. Reusing the available
libdw/libelf development headers allowed the frozen source/test payload to
build and pass.

This is a stream-ordering correctness change, not a performance claim or a
full-model/training/backward validation.

DeepEP V2.5 introduces dedicated communication buffers for EP, PP, Engram, and bucket collectives, together with new primitives for redundant-expert load balancing. GPU kernels are now compiled through DeepJIT, while installation builds the host C++ extension.
This release also fully removes V1 and its NVSHMEM dependency.
New Features
Dedicated buffer APIs
@LyricZhao
Split ElasticBuffer into EPBuffer, EngramBuffer, PPBuffer, and BucketBuffer, sharing the BufferBase lifecycle.
Add BufferAllocator for planning symmetric tensor allocations before buffer construction.
Expert load balancing
@cqzhangyu
@LyricZhao
Add EPBuffer.lb_prefetch_weights to transfer expert weights and quantization scales to redundant expert slots over NVLink.
Add EPBuffer.lb_reduce_grads to accumulate redundant experts’ FP32 gradients into the original experts.
These primitives support the dynamic expert-replication approach explored by MoonEP and UltraEP. Replication planning and token rerouting are supplied by the integrating framework.
Bucket collectives for CP and DP
@jason-huang03
@bucket-xv
@cqzhangyu
@dromniscience
@sphish
Batched all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-reduce across NVLink, RDMA, and hybrid domains.
Sessions for communicating ordinary PyTorch tensors through temporary bucket storage.
EP improvements
@LyricZhao
Deferred dispatch/combine epilogues for communication-computation overlap.
Cached expanded layouts and zero padding between experts.
Engram
@tianr22
@sphish
Multi-layer storage on GPU or CPU, with one completion hook per layer.
Build and runtime
@LyricZhao
Move GPU kernel compilation to DeepJIT.
Remove installation-time NVCC compilation and GPU architecture selection.
Notes
Migrate from ElasticBuffer to the dedicated buffer APIs.
V1 APIs, legacy documentation, and NVSHMEM support have been removed.
Bucket collectives, Engram, and PP remain experimental.
Requires NVIDIA Hopper or newer GPUs, CUDA 13.1+, NCCL 2.32.3+, PyTorch 2.10+ with CUDA support, Python 3.10+, and a C++20 compiler.

title: Document and test ordinary sync-free receive tensor lifetimes
body:
## Summary

Document and exercise the lifetime contract of **ordinary independently allocated receive outputs** from compact `dispatch(do_cpu_sync=False)`.

- Add a README paragraph explaining valid receive prefixes, output ownership versus stream readiness, the explicit ready-event/`record_stream` handoff, and why a prefix view retains the full capacity allocation.
- Add a 166-line standalone native regression for saved-view backward after later dispatches and delayed cross-stream consumers under allocator pressure.

No production Python/C++/CUDA implementation, default, or API changes. The internal dispatch copy epilogue still runs. This is not borrowed communication-buffer storage or a zero-copy dispatch implementation.

## Regression coverage

The new `tests/ep/test_recv_lifetime.py` uses the independent NCCL dispatch reference and requires bitwise equality of payloads, local expert indices, routing weights, source-token metadata, and the saved-activation weight gradient.

Each process run covers:

- Deterministic dispatch off/on; output allocation on the compute/communication stream.
- Uneven inputs, balanced routes, masked routes, and highly skewed routing with empty receivers.
- Two selected experts on the same destination rank, distinguishing unique receive rows from token/expert assignments.
- A prefix saved with `ctx.save_for_backward`, followed by three additional dispatches through the same buffer before backward.
- A delayed reader on another stream, dropping the original receive allocation references and allocating/filling four same-capacity tensors on the allocation stream. The copy destination and allocator warm-up are prepared before the delay. Pressure writes must finish while a **pre-read** event is still pending; a pending post-copy event alone is insufficient.

Scheduling can miss the pressure window. All ranks agree on numerical correctness and window validity, then retry in collective lockstep with a longer delay (at most three attempts). Actual corruption fails immediately; an inconclusive window is never silently reported as coverage.

The consumer handoff uses a CUDA event captured **after the first dispatch-event wait**, including its deterministic-sort hook. It does not depend on repeated waits on the original `EventOverlap`; that is separate from this lifetime coverage.

## Validation

### Current polished revision

Head: `97fa6d18ff717df99acbdbb862325bda3d4a0d46`, based on public main `b5a33eefda39485f438dc764695b71ba7b9249b6`.

The current 166-line test passed on H200 with PyTorch `2.13.0+cu132`, CUDA 13.2 and NCCL 2.32.3. Each native lifetime policy was run once with eight ranks: 24 distributed saved-prefix/backward cases in total, with 24 valid delayed-consumer allocator-pressure windows. This is positive coverage of the current reorganized test; the historical negative and scheduling controls below were not rerun against this revision.

```bash
EP_AVOID_RECORD_STREAM=0 python tests/ep/test_recv_lifetime.py --num-processes 8 --num-tokens 64 --hidden 512
EP_AVOID_RECORD_STREAM=1 python tests/ep/test_recv_lifetime.py --num-processes 8 --num-tokens 64 --hidden 512
```

### Historical validation of the earlier test version

Tested commit: `01c31d0d75f155ca00ba933a6b9ab7a01459169e`, based on upstream `93eb6eb238127e96c6d7a4a625a6dad158348509`. The results in this subsection belong to that earlier test version, not to a rerun of the current 166-line test.

One node, eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs in a single NVLink domain; PyTorch `2.13.0+cu132`, CUDA runtime 13.2, loaded NCCL 2.32.3. The unchanged upstream native extension and the tested source archive/test-file hashes were verified. No borrowed-view implementation or event-wrapper patch was included.

Both native lifetime policies were run in fresh processes, three repeats each, using the same two command lines above.

Validation controls: `EP_DISABLE_GIN=1`, `EP_REUSE_NCCL_COMM=0`, `EP_BUFFER_DEBUG=0`, `NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=none`, `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8`. Seed 42; deterministic PyTorch algorithms enabled with uninitialized-memory filling disabled.

| Native record-stream policy | Fresh repeats per arm | Positive rank/cases | Exact saved-view gradients | Deleted-record rejections | Forced-retry passes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `EP_AVOID_RECORD_STREAM=0` | 3 | 288/288 | 288/288 | 96/96 | 96/96 |
| `EP_AVOID_RECORD_STREAM=1` | 3 | 288/288 | 288/288 | 96/96 | 96/96 |

Two additional controls were run outside the PR using that exact earlier public test source, without changing DeepEP's implementation:

- **Negative control:** AST-remove exactly the consumer-side `prefix.record_stream(reader)` expression from `cross_stream_pressure`. For balanced nonempty receives, run both deterministic modes and both allocation streams. All 24 distributed cases were rejected by the specific `CROSS_STREAM_RECEIVE_MISMATCH` assertion; actual local data corruption was observed in all 192 rank/cases. Other assertions or an ineffective window do not count as detection.
- **Scheduling control:** synchronize only rank 0 immediately before its first `pending_before` query. All ranks must retry attempt 0 together and pass on a later effective attempt. All 24 distributed cases / 192 rank/cases passed.

An earlier draft's post-copy-event stress missed the deleted-record mutation. That draft is not the sensitivity evidence above; the pre-read/completed-pressure ordering and destination preallocation were added before rerunning all historical arms.

All eighteen historical fresh launches exited successfully. Source/input hashes, exact per-rank coverage, control mutation identities and completion/exit sentinels were audited from downloaded logs. Archive SHA256: `834a31fa761e439678244ae49cdaf98491ead5fb23b4724500ba038366eac777`.

Local checks for that earlier revision: Python compilation, Ruff 0.6.5, YAPF 0.40.2 (no diff), and `git diff --check` passed.

## Scope

This establishes component lifetime/gradient correctness for ordinary compact BF16 receives in one physical NVLink domain. It does not establish full-model convergence, training throughput gains, borrowed-storage safety, FP8/expanded layouts, or multi-node hybrid routing. Capacity-retention assertions deliberately distinguish logical tensor bytes from retained storage bytes.

With the evolution of hardware, networking, and model architectures, the previous DeepEP V1 had accumulated too much legacy baggage and performance issues. Today, we are excited to introduce
DeepEP V2
, which includes a complete refactoring of Expert Parallelism — achieving extreme performance with several times fewer SM resources compared to V1, while supporting significantly larger scale-up and scale-out domains — as well as experimental 0 SM Engram, 0 SM Pipeline Parallelism, and 0 SM Context Parallelism all-gather.
We are also happy to announce that we have switched from the NVSHMEM backend to the more lightweight
NCCL Gin backend
.
New Features
Fully JIT (Just-In-Time compilation)
NCCL Gin backend
Header-only & lightweight
Able to reuse existing NCCL communicators
EPv2
CUDA graph compatible, or faster CPU sync in saving memory mode
High-throughput and low-latency APIs unified into a single interface, with a new GEMM layout
Larger scale-up & scale-out domain support (up to EP2048)
Analytical SM & QP count calculation — no more auto-tuning needed
Both hybrid & direct modes remain supported
For V3-like legacy training, SM usage reduced from 24 to 4 - 6 while maintaining equivalent or better performance
0 SM Engram (with RDMA)
0 SM PP (with RDMA)
0 SM CP (with Copy Engine)
Notes
Buffer size consumption is larger than V1
0 SM RDMA low-latency EP is no longer supported
Engram, PP, and CP are experimental features
Still On-going Features
Elastic GPU & CPU buffers
: A contiguous virtual address space that maps to a hybrid of GPU and CPU physical memory under the hood, enabling fully automatic and transparent Engram or imbalanced EP
Reducing intermediate buffer sizes by leveraging EP replay to handle load imbalance
All-gather updates and reduce-scatter implementations for DP & TP
Performance
Following V3's configuration, we tested with 8K tokens per batch, 7168 hidden dimensions, top 8 experts, FP8 dispatching, and BF16 combining, and obtained the following results:

moe: add DeepEP V2 ElasticBuffer probe and opt-in buffer path
…
1d6b522
DeepEP V2 (
deepseek-ai/DeepEP#605
, merged 2026-04-29) introduces
`ElasticBuffer` alongside the legacy `Buffer`. Both classes are
exported from `deep_ep.__init__`, so SGLang's existing V1 code path
continues to work unchanged on a V2 install.

This patch adds a second import probe (`have_deepep_v2`) next to the
existing `use_deepep` flag, then lets users opt in to the V2
`ElasticBuffer` ctor behind `SGLANG_DEEPEP_USE_V2=1`. The V1 path is
byte-identical when the env var is unset, so this is a backwards-
compatible addition.

V2 collapses the V1 NVL/RDMA byte-pool ctor into a single MoE-shape
ctor and derives the internal buffer size from `num_max_tokens_per_rank`,
`hidden`, and `num_topk`. `num_allocated_qps=0` asks V2 to auto-size
and auto-cap the Queue-Pair budget on AWS EFA (the 128-slot GIN ring
ceiling; see `_is_efa_fabric` in `deep_ep/buffers/elastic.py`).

Why:
- Removes the need for users to monkeypatch `deep_ep.Buffer` to reach
  V2 semantics, and mirrors the probe shape already used in
  NVIDIA/Megatron-LM's `fused_a2a.py` (`HAVE_DEEP_EP_V2`). Opt-in
  env-var gate keeps the change infra-bump-shaped, not a default
  switch flip.
- vLLM is landing a parallel native-V2 path in
vllm-project/vllm#41183
(16 commits, active review). SGLang users
  running mixed-framework MoE stacks benefit from having V2 reachable
  in SGLang without a runtime monkeypatch.

V2 parity rules baked in:
- `num_max_tokens_per_rank` sourced from
  `envs.SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK` when the
  caller did not pin it (matches the V1 low-latency path).
- `num_topk=0` at ctor time: DeepEP V2 accepts this and derives a
  conservative group-size-based hint, so we don't need to know the
  router topk at buffer construction.
- `clean_buffer()` skips the legacy `clean_low_latency_buffer` call
  when the underlying buffer is an ElasticBuffer (no equivalent on
  V2, per `deep_ep/buffers/elastic.py`).

Warp-specialized architecture for the SM90 FP8 MQA logits kernel.
Replaces the production post-processing path (SHFL+STG inline) with
an epilogue warpgroup that runs overlapped with the next kv-block.

Architecture: 4 TC WGs (512) + 1 Epi WG (128) + 1 TMA WG (128) = 768 threads.
TC does dual-bank WGMMA (N=64 split, warpgroup_wait<1> overlap) +
partial reduce → STS to epi_buf in SMEM. Epi does LDS → horizontal
sum → STG to global. TMA is unchanged.

Key design decisions:
- TC@104 regs (0 spill): full weights[32] preload with scale_kv
  deferred to between empty_epi wait and warpgroup_wait<1>
- kNumEpiStages=3 matching kNumKVStages to prevent inter-WG
  pipeline desynchronization
- epi_buf stride = BLOCK_Q*4+1 (17) for bank conflict reduction
- Bootstrap guard uses (num_total_kv_blocks | kv_block_idx) != 0
  instead of a persistent boolean to save 1 register

JIT launcher changes (SM90 path only):
- 12-parameter template with kNumEpiStages=3
- SMEM includes epi_buf (3 stages × BLOCK_KV × stride × sizeof(float))
- Thread count: num_math_threads + num_epi_threads + num_tma_threads

Performance (342 configs, H200 SXM):
  Speedup vs production: mean 1.065x, min 1.027x, max 1.111x
  Regressions: 0 out of 342
  Correctness: 295/295 full test configs pass

title: github:deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM:325 fetched implementation patch
[Feat]Add native FP8 Tensor Core GEMM support for SM89 (Ada Lovelace)
body:
**Title**  
Add native FP8 Tensor Core GEMM support for SM89 (Ada Lovelace)

**Body**

## Summary

This change adds a native FP8 Tensor Core GEMM for SM89 (Ada Lovelace). SM89 is the first architecture below Hopper that has FP8 Tensor Cores.

Previously, SM80 and SM89 used the same path. The path required SM90 or higher for FP8. This was correct for SM80 because Ampere has no FP8 Tensor Cores. It was wrong for SM89. SM89 implements the instruction `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` (`QMMA.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3`). The change separates the two architectures and gives SM89 a real kernel.

## Why

- SM89 has FP8 Tensor Cores. It does not have the SM90 features (no TMA, no `mbarrier.try_wait.parity`, no WGMMA, no clusters). It could not reuse the SM90 or SM100 kernels. It fell back to BF16 through cuBLASLt.
- FP8 users on Ada had to dequantize and run BF16. They lost about 2× of Tensor Core throughput.
- The shared SM80/SM89 path also gave wrong error messages. An SM89 user saw a message that did not apply to their GPU.

## Design

SM89 has no TMA and no asynchronous barriers. The kernel uses the pre-Hopper primitives.

- It uses `mma.sync` (wrapped in `deep_gemm/mma/sm89.cuh`, with A/B/C fragment layouts documented) and `ldmatrix.x4` for operand staging.
- It uses a multi-stage `cp.async` pipeline with a 128-byte XOR swizzle.
- It uses a persistent block scheduler (one CTA per SM). Tiles walk in a loop.
- It uses direct global stores because SM89 has no TMA store. It has an alignment-safe scalar tail. An MMA lane owns a pair of adjacent columns. For odd N the element offset of a row can be odd. A 2-element vector store is then illegal. This caused the original misaligned address failure.
- Block K is fixed at 128 because of the per-128-channel scaling granularity. Pipeline depth and tile shapes come from a new cost model in `csrc/jit_kernels/heuristics/sm89.hpp`. The warp split uses one shared function `get_mma_sync_warps_n()`. Host heuristics and device code both call it so they cannot disagree.

Both SM90 SF recipes are supported:  
`(1, 1, 128)` (per-token A and B scales) and  
`(1, 128, 128)` (per-token A, one B scale per 128-column N block).  
The second recipe is the default when FP32 scales are used. SM89 uses the same FP32 SF layouts as SM90. The function `transform_sf_into_required_layout` was extended. It was not duplicated.

## Scope

Supported features:  
dense FP8 GEMM, K-major (NT) operands only, FP32 and BF16 outputs, `D = C + A @ B`, ragged M/N, `k % 16 == 0`, both aliases (`fp8_fp4_gemm_nt`, `fp8_gemm_nt`, `fp4_gemm_nt`), and shape specialization.

Still rejected (with an explicit message that names the requirement):  
grouped and K-grouped FP8, MN-major FP8 operands, FP4, custom epilogues, `alpha` scaling, PDL, and MQA/attention.  
BF16 keeps its cuBLASLt fallback.

## Incidental fixes

- `set_pdl()` now panics below SM90. It no longer sets a flag that `griddepcontrol` cannot honour.  
  `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` is wrapped in a no-op below `__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900` so the SF-layout kernels compile for SM89.
- `call_cublaslt_api` used `CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_TF32` for non-FP32 operands. That mode only down-casts FP32 inputs to TF32. BF16/FP8 operands ran at TF32 precision by mistake. Now only FP32 inputs use that mode.
- A new `DG_PANIC` macro throws always and carries a message.

## Bug found during validation

The persistent loop primed its `cp.async` pipeline only in the prologue before the tile loop. It relied on a cross-tile tail load to prime the next tile. A tile’s tail can only reach the stages that are already free of the current tile — prologue stages `p ∈ [0, kNumStages-2-num_k_blocks]`. The next tile’s K loop consumes `p = 0..num_k_blocks-1`. When `num_k_blocks < kNumStages-1` (example: `k=512`, 4 blocks, 8 stages) the high stages were never reloaded. The next tile read the previous tile’s shared memory. Symptom: non-deterministic `nan` and values near 1e30. The problem appeared only for small M spread over many N tiles.

The fix extracts the prologue into `prime_pipeline()` and re-primes unconditionally after the epilogue. The re-prime is guarded by `cp_async_wait<0>()` and a `__syncthreads()`. `cp.async` completion is per-thread, so both are required before the stages can be reused. The change removes a prologue/epilogue overlap that was never correct. Measured cost is about 0–3.5 % (4096³: 2518 µs vs 2507 µs, within noise; 4096×4096×512: 420 µs vs 405 µs).

`tests/test_sm89.py` added the shapes `(1, 4096, 512)`, `(64, 4096, 512)` and `(128, 4096, 128)`. Reverting the fix makes these tests fail (34 failures). They are real regression tests.

## Testing

Hardware: RTX 4060 Laptop (SM89, 24 SMs, 7.6 GiB), CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130.

- `tests/test_sm89.py` — 17 tests, OK from a cold JIT cache (~130 s).  
  Covers both recipes × both output dtypes × accumulate × 12 shapes, explicit `recipe=(1,128,128)`, `recipe_a`/`recipe_b` pairs, entry-point aliases, compiled-dim specialization, bitwise determinism across repeats, accumulation-versus-zero-C equivalence, BF16 GEMM and all its layouts, cuBLASLt FP8/BF16, SF layout kernels, and one rejection case per unsupported feature.
- `tests/test_layout.py` — OK.
- Upstream `tests/test_fp8_fp4.py::test_gemm` — OK.  
  The upstream shape grid reaches m=129280 / n=7168 and OOMs on a 7.6 GiB card. Shapes were clamped to m≤4096, n≤4096, k≤1280 by monkey-patching `enumerate_normal` in a throw-away driver. The test body, recipes and assertions were not changed.
- Upstream `tests/test_bf16.py::test_gemm` — correctness OK, same clamping.  
  The perf-print block was stubbed because `bench_kineto` matches on the kernel name `bf16_gemm`, which does not exist on SM89 (BF16 goes through the cuBLASLt fallback). All `diff < 1e-5` assertions ran without change.
- Other suites fail only for environmental reasons and are unchanged by this PR:  
  `test_einsum` raises the intended “Unsupported architecture”,  
  `test_lazy_init` and `test_locality_domain` need multiple GPUs,  
  `test_bf16` / `test_legacy` OOM at upstream shapes.

Throughput, single GPU, FP8 in / BF16 out:

| m    | n    | k    | time      | TFLOPS |
|------|------|------|-----------|--------|
| 1    | 4096 | 4096 | 33.6 µs   | 1.0    |
| 128  | 4096 | 4096 | 168.4 µs  | 25.5   |
| 4096 | 4096 | 4096 | 2517.8 µs | 54.6   |
| 4096 | 4096 | 512  | 419.7 µs  | 40.9   |

Problem
deep_jit::cuda::Device::get_prop()
calls
cudaFree(nullptr)
once to make sure the CUDA context exists.
cudaFree
is prohibited while a stream is being captured in the global or thread-local mode. If the first device query happens inside a capture, it fails with
cudaErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported
(900), DeepJIT panics, and the capture is invalidated (
cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated
, 901, at
cudaStreamEndCapture
).
Libraries hit this through lazy initialization: the runtime created by
create_lazy_jit
queries the device on first use. With DeepGEMM
main
(which pins DeepJIT
e5bdee2
), the first DeepGEMM call in a process fails if it happens inside
torch.cuda.graph
with the default capture mode:
Panic error (third-party/deep_jit/include/deep_jit/backend/cuda/device.hpp:15): cudaFree(nullptr) failed with CUDA error 900 (cudaErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported): operation not permitted when stream is capturing
  #0 deep_jit::cuda::Device::get_prop() at third-party/deep_jit/include/deep_jit/backend/cuda/device.hpp:15
  #1 deep_jit::cuda::CompilerOptions::default_options(deep_jit::Env const&, deep_jit::cuda::Device&) at third-party/deep_jit/include/deep_jit/backend/cuda/device.hpp:62
  #2 ... deep_gemm::init_jit(...)::{lambda} ...
  #3 deep_jit::LazyInit<deep_jit::Runtime<deep_jit::CUDA> >::operator->()
This is the only blocker I found. Once the runtime has been initialized, compiling and loading a new kernel during a global-mode capture already works.
Fix
Add a small RAII guard that switches the calling thread to
cudaStreamCaptureModeRelaxed
with
cudaThreadExchangeStreamCaptureMode
, and use it only around the one-time initialization in
get_prop()
. The previous mode is restored when the guard goes out of scope. This is the same mechanism as PyTorch's
c10::cuda::CUDAStreamCaptureModeGuard
, kept local so that
device.hpp
does not depend on c10.

Device
is queried for the first time inside a global, thread-local and relaxed capture.
A runtime from
create_lazy_jit

title: [SM90] Add optimized SM90 support.
body:
## Summary

This PR adds an optimized SM90 build and runtime path for Hopper GPUs such as H20 and H100, while preserving the existing SM100/SM103 defaults.

SM90 uses an 8-CTA cluster for small-batch, long-sequence BF16 Top-K workloads. The cluster path is enabled from a vocabulary size of 128K, based on measurements on an 8×H20 machine. SM100 and SM103 continue to use the existing 16-CTA cluster and 512K threshold.

## Changes

- Add `DEEP_SELECT_CUDA_ARCHS` to select `90a`, `100a`, and/or `103a` at build time.
- Keep the default build targets unchanged: `sm_100a` and `sm_103a`.
- Add eight SM90 cluster instantiations covering:
  - `int32` and `int64` output indices
  - `sorted_index` enabled and disabled
  - `return_value` enabled and disabled
- Dispatch SM90 BF16 workloads to an 8-CTA cluster when:
  - `batch_size <= 6`
  - `vocab_size >= 128K`
  - `topk <= 1024`
- Preserve the existing 16-CTA cluster and 512K threshold for SM100/SM103.
- Fall back to `nvidia-smi -L` for CUDA platform detection when `lspci` is unavailable in a container.
- Avoid the `std::format` dependency in the C++ binding so the extension builds with older host standard libraries commonly found in CUDA containers.
- Document the SM90 build command:

```bash
DEEP_SELECT_CUDA_ARCHS=90a pip install -v .
```

## Performance

Measured on NVIDIA H20 with BF16 input, `batch_size` 1 and 6, and `topk` 512 and 1024. Each result is the median of 100 cold-cache runs.

The improvement column compares the new 8-CTA cluster with the existing single-CTA path compiled for SM90.

| Vocabulary size | Improvement over single CTA | Speedup over `torch.topk` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 128K | 25.2%–35.0% | 3.11×–3.83× |
| 256K | 36.5%–44.6% | 2.79×–3.57× |
| 512K | 52.4%–56.1% | 2.66×–3.75× |
| 1M | 61.5%–62.3% | 2.12×–4.11× |

Short-sequence and large-batch workloads continue to use the existing normal kernel. Their measured speedup over `torch.topk` remains 4.88×–6.27×.

## Validation

- Clean SM90 build with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.11.
- `cuobjdump` register-spill check passed with no spills.
- 20/20 targeted correctness cases passed.
- Coverage included:
  - normal and 8-CTA cluster paths
  - BF16 and FP32 inputs
  - `int32` and `int64` indices
  - `sorted_index`
  - optional value output
  - variable row lengths through `end`
  - per-row index offsets
- The final performance matrix passed Top-K value-set validation against `torch.topk` for every case.

Summary
This PR adds an opt-in, two-stage packed selected-KV sparse decode path for the
GLM-5.2 / V3.2 FP8 MLA format on SM90:
pack_selected_kv
gathers selected records from the paged KV cache into an
opaque tile-major workspace.
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
consumes that workspace with a packed
sparse-decode specialization that avoids sparse index and page translation
on the attention critical path.
The existing native sparse-decode API and dispatch remain unchanged. The new
path is explicitly restricted to SM90 and is not enabled automatically.
Note
Alternative host-offload path (not part of this pr):
The packed interface also enables a separate offload path in which gathering and packing are performed on the host, followed by transferring only the packed selected-KV workspace to the device. In this case, the full KV caches of the shared layers no longer need to remain resident in HBM. This can substantially expand KV-cache capacity.
Since this implementation introduces a compile-time packed-KV specialization in the existing SM90 sparse decode kernel, I’d appreciate maintainers’ guidance on whether you prefer the current shared-kernel approach, a policy/loader-based abstraction, or a separate packed-kernel implementation; I’m happy to restructure it in a follow-up revision based on your feedback.
Motivation
GLM-5.2 can share selected physical indices across multiple MLA layers. When
those indices are available before the layer that consumes them, the runtime
can move sparse address resolution and KV gathering into an earlier overlap
window.
The attention kernel can then read a contiguous packed workspace instead of
repeatedly:
loading and validating physical indices;
translating indices into page and in-page coordinates;
constructing unrelated global addresses; and
gathering NoPE, scale, and RoPE components from the paged cache.
Packing and attention are intentionally separate operations so a runtime can
overlap packing with preceding work such as MoE communication.
What changed
SM90 packing kernel
pack_selected_kv
copies each selected 656-byte V3.2 record byte-for-byte:
512-byte FP8 E4M3 NoPE data;
16-byte FP32 scales; and
128-byte BF16 RoPE data.
The packer writes an opaque 64-token tile-major workspace. It supports a valid
selected-index prefix described by
topk_length
and zero-fills invalid suffix
records.
Callers may provide reusable contiguous
uint8
storage using
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
.
Packed attention specialization
The packed H=64 and H=128 instantiations reuse FlashMLA's existing:
WGMMA and dequantization pipeline;
online softmax;
DSM clustering for H=128;
split accumulation;
epilogue; and
combine kernel.
The specialization replaces the sparse index/page/gather loader with direct
tile-major loads and preserves partial-tail masking.
Scheduler policy
H=128 uses the same scheduler as native sparse decode.
H=64 uses the compact request-local scheduler selected by the L20X
experiments. For the measured full-prefix
topk=2048
, 132-SM
B*S_q=16
regime, it falls back to the faster native scheduler.
This scheduler is used only by the opt-in packed helper and does not change
native sparse decode. The benchmark includes an identical-scheduler control to
isolate the packed-load kernel gain.
Python API
This PR adds:
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
get_packed_mla_metadata
pack_selected_kv
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
Supported scope
The initial path is intentionally limited to:
SM90;
V3.2 FP8 sparse KV records;
d_qk=576
;
d_v=512
;
H in {64, 128}
;
MQA KV; and
top-k capacity divisible by 64.
The API fails closed for unsupported architectures and shapes. SM100 is not
enabled because this implementation has only been evaluated on SM90.
L20X results
The repository-local benchmark was run on an NVIDIA L20X with 132 SMs using:
CUDA 13.0;
PyTorch 2.13.0;
topk=2048
;
B={1,2,4,7,8}
;
S_q={1,2,3,4,8,16}
;
H={64,128}
;
request-disjoint physical KV ranges;
a 512 MiB L2 flush before each measured path;
10 warmups and 200 timed repetitions; and
60 total cases.
Comparison
Geometric-mean speedup
Wins
Packed attention, identical scheduler
1.098x
60/60
Integrated packed attention stage
1.115x
60/60
Integrated H=64 cohort
1.131x
30/30
H=128 cohort, native scheduler
1.100x
30/30
Pack + attention without overlap
0.740x
0/60
Packing is excluded from the attention-stage comparisons.
The unhidden result is included deliberately: this path is useful only when
the runtime can move most packing work outside the attention critical path.
This PR does not add automatic dispatch or change the default native path.
The H=64 hybrid policy selected the tuned scheduler in 26 cases and the native
fallback in four cases. The four fallback cases improved by approximately
6.5% to 7.4% compared with using the tuned scheduler unconditionally.
Correctness and benchmark coverage
python tests/test_flash_mla_packed_sparse_decoding.py
python benchmark/bench_flash_mla_packed_sparse_decode.py \
  --output packed_sparse_decode_latency.csv
The correctness test passes five cases covering:
a single full boundary tile;
H=64 partial tails and heterogeneous active lengths;
the H=64 native-scheduler fallback;
full production top-k with H=128; and
H=128 heterogeneous partial tails.
The tests compare both output and LSE with native sparse decode and verify the
packed workspace layout.
Observed result:
passed 5 packed sparse-decode cases
The new CUDA kernels compiled for SM90 without register spills. The packer
used 18 registers, and both packed-attention instantiations used 168 registers.
Runtime follow-up
This PR contains the two FlashMLA kernels needed for the packed path, but
intentionally does not include current-token runtime orchestration.
A future vLLM integration can:
pack historical records early into caller-managed storage;
overwrite any selected current-token record after its KV becomes available,
for example with a scatter operation;
synchronize the packing/update stream with attention; and
select native fallback when the expected overlap is insufficient.
Workspace pooling, CUDA stream placement, current-token updates, overlap
eligibility, and end-to-end TPOT measurements belong to that runtime
integration.
For
topk=2048
, the workspace requires approximately 1.281 MiB per query row,
so runtime dispatch should also enforce a workspace budget.
Non-goals
This PR does not:
replace or modify the behavior of native sparse decode;
enable the packed path by default;
add SM100 support;
claim an end-to-end speedup without concurrent runtime integration; or
include current-token patch orchestration.
setup.py
is changed only to register the three new CUDA source files.

Summary
This PR adds optional per-request
topk_length
support to the SM90
DeepSeek-V3.2 FP8 sparse decode kernel (
d_qk=576
). SM90 V3.2 can now use
dynamic top-k instead of always processing the full allocated top-k capacity.
When
topk_length
is provided, the kernel:
loads the valid length for each batch row;
schedules only
max(ceil_div(topk_length, TOPK_BLOCK_SIZE), 1)
blocks;
masks a partial tail before its indices can be used for KV addressing; and
includes the absolute top-k position in the softmax validity predicate.
When
topk_length == nullptr
, the existing fixed top-k behavior is preserved.
There is no public API change, and MODEL1 and SM100 behavior are unchanged.
Why
template<bool DYNAMIC_TOPK, ...>
I also tested a single-device-kernel implementation that checks
params.topk_length != nullptr
at runtime. The condition is grid-uniform, but
the compiler cannot remove the length load, tail predicates, extra control
flow, or their value lifetimes from the fixed path.
template<bool DYNAMIC_TOPK>
moves the choice to host launch dispatch:
false
: the dynamic-length logic is compiled out, preserving the fixed path;
true
: per-row block counts and partial-tail safety checks are enabled.
The comparison implementation is available at
7b7c831
on
test/sm90-v32-dynamic-topk-runtime-device
. It regresses the representative
B64-B128 fixed cases by 8.4%-9.4%, while the specialized implementation stays
within 0.5% of the baseline. Both builds report 168 registers, 12 barriers,
and no spills, so the generated hot-path instructions—not an occupancy

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash stores each KV token as 528B: 512B of FP8 E4M3 covering
the full 512-wide K (rope lanes quantized, no BF16 rope segment) plus a 16B
footer of 16 UE8M0 scales over 32-wide groups (the
deepseek-ai/FlashMLA#221
layout, SM100-only there). Add ModelType::DSV4_1 on top of the ScaleSpec
groundwork: GLM53_NOPE-style geometry (D_ROPE=0) composed with a 32-wide
UE8M0 footer.

Kernel side the format is simpler than DSV4 (one 512B bulk per row, a single
unified block-scaled FP8 QK pass, no rope MMA paths). The two new mechanics:

- the 16B footer row generalizes the scale gather from one uint64_t to a
  width-selected load (uint4) in both the prefill IO helper and the decode
  kernel's staged gather;
- the 32-wide groups constrain the XV W-fold (one scale group per W buffer),
  so an 8-warp XV split would floor NT_PER_WARP_XV to 0: decode runs a
  4-math-warp tile at BI=64 (the DOTS3_SWA halving precedent) and prefill is
  SG-only on the BI=32 producer/consumer tile. The ComputeTraits/SmemLayout
  aliases now take the XV warp count so the NT_PER_WARP_XV assert evaluates at
  the warp count the XV MMA actually runs at.

Selection is explicit everywhere (d_qk=512 collides with DSV4, the 528B
payload with GLM53_NOPE): the functional API gains kv_scale_format=
"ue8m0_g32", the TRTLLM-compat entry kv_cache_format="fp8_dsv41", and the
decode-dsv4 FFI takes an explicit model_type (-1 keeps the legacy width
inference, matching the paged-entry kAuto convention). Dual-cache decode is
supported like DSV4; dual-cache prefill (MG_DUAL) is intentionally not
instantiated. Calibration keys a new dsv4_1 family at topk 512.

Tests: decode matrix (dedicated/runtime-H heads, partial-tail topk, sinks),
SG prefill, dual-cache through the TRTLLM entry, poisoned-slot-0 NaN safety
on both gather paths, dispatch/plan/envelope coverage. 666 passed on RTX PRO
6000 (SM120).

title: [SDSA 3/7] Add paged MQA logits for an indexer with one head (BF16 keys)
body:
DSA-style sparse attention uses an indexer to pick each query token's Top-K keys. `fp8_paged_mqa_logits` scores keys for an indexer with many heads. This PR adds `single_head_paged_mqa_logits` for an indexer with one head. Its score is the dot product of a query row and a key, with no head weights and no ReLU.

The keys are BF16, with 128 dimensions, in pages of 64 keys. Each request has 1 to 8 query rows, such as a decode token and its draft tokens. The kernel is a warp-specialized SM100 kernel. Its grid size comes from the context capacity, not the lengths, so the call can be captured in a CUDA graph.

On GB200 (NVFP4 keys, 16-128 requests, 32K-1M keys), this grid was up to 15% faster than a grid sized from the actual lengths. It was 3% slower in the worst case.

Part 3 of 7 of SDSA. SDSA is sparse attention with a one-head indexer that picks each query token's Top-K keys, and an MQA core that attends to them. This stack adds it in 7 PRs: token-sparse attention for MQA/GQA (1-2), then the single-head indexer (3-7).

Previous: #6421 (2/7) Add key unions and masks so dense attention kernels can run token-sparse attention. Only this PR's last commit is new.

Next: #6423 (4/7) Support NVFP4 keys in the one-head paged MQA logits, and write them to the paged cache.

![Where this PR sits in the SDSA stack](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/netanel-haber/flashinfer/sdsa-stack-diagrams/sdsa-stack-3.png)

AI assistance was used.

title: feat(topk_varlen): exact CuTe-DSL primitives top-k backends with fused page-table output (Ampere and newer)
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Exact, single-launch top-k for the DeepSeek sparse-attention (DSA) indexer, as four new
`top_k_varlen` backends plus a fused paged output, with Ampere and newer as the floor instead
of Blackwell only.

**New backends** (all CuTe-DSL *primitives* kernels: raw pointers, integer address math,
`cute.arch` PTX wrappers; no layout algebra, so one source compiles for sm_80 through sm_120
and Rubin):

- `walkfirst_primitives` — the decode default. A replica-deterministic sample sets a value
  threshold and a 256-bin scale; every CTA walks its slice once; the last-arriving CTA merges
  the bin-major publish tables and resolves the crossing bin with an exact key-space select.
  Rows up to 16K columns never enter that pipeline: a census arm (<= 4K) and a register-resident
  arm (4K to 16K) solve them in one CTA. Floods past the tie capacity are refined from the
  crossing bin's exact key range; anything else falls through to a fused exact re-solve on
  device, so every call stays sync-free and CUDA-graph capturable.
- `radix_primitives` — SGLang's coarse-histogram structure made exact (no tie truncation),
  fp32/fp16/bf16, grouped rows (`next_n`) and compressed columns (`compress_ratio`), optional
  values, multi-CTA long rows.
- `cutlass_primitives` — the vendored cutlass-primitives library (`VENDORED.md`, Apache-2.0):
  register, clustered-register and streaming kernels with a census split for large k; the
  full-row leader. `flashinfer.topk_varlen` exports its workspace helpers
  (`cutlass_primitives_workspace_bytes`, `cutlass_primitives_row_order`) and
  `release_cutlass_primitives_resources`.
- `sglang` — SGLang's own DeepSeek-V4 indexer top-k (Apache-2.0, vendored verbatim from upstream
  commit 7f27bf4708; `csrc/sglang_dsv4/VENDORED.md`, `licenses/LICENSE.sglang.txt`) under the
  same contract, including a paged variant: the same kernel SGLang runs, for parity and for the
  check that the FlashInfer API adds no overhead over the raw kernel. It is exact only while the
  rank-k bin holds at most 2048 candidates, so `auto` never selects it.

**Fused paged output.** `top_k_varlen(..., page_table=table, page_size=64)` returns physical
KV slots `page_table[q, c // page_size] * page_size + c % page_size` from the selection launch
itself (the SGLang DSA decode contract, one kernel instead of a top-k plus a transform pass).
The table is a contiguous, 16-byte-aligned int32 `(requests, max_pages)` tensor covering every
request's valid length; it may be narrower than the logits width, and rows past its coverage
are clamped to the covered prefix. Served by `walkfirst_primitives`, `radix_primitives` and
`sglang`; `backend="auto"` with a page table ranks the two exact primitives backends (they are
outside the unpaged ranking).

**Also in this PR:** a fix to the pre-existing multi-CTA `radix` kernel (chunks shorter than
their misaligned prefix read past the valid length and wrote shared memory at negative offsets;
CTA 0 could reset the group's arrival counter while a time-sliced peer still spun on it; the
per-group state grows by one int, STATE_SIZE 770 to 771, allocated internally with a bumped
cache key), the trace template for `top_k_varlen` extended with the paged inputs (the page size
names the paged definitions), the benchmarks that produced the numbers below, the four new
backends in `benchmarks/routines/topk_varlen.py`, and a one-line fix to
`tests/trace/example.py` (an upstream call passed a `str` device to `is_sm100a_supported`, which
crashes the example on sm_100 hosts).

**Why.** The DSA indexer runs one top-k per layer per decode step; SGLang today uses its own
fused kernel. These backends are exact where that kernel approximates, faster on every decode
cell we measured across six architectures, and fuse the page-table output so an engine needs
one launch. Measurements (`benchmarks/bench_topk_replay_ties.py`, CUDA-graph replay, 16 rows,
K 512, fp32, rows from a recorded DeepSeek decode trace of 500 to 2100 columns in a 16K buffer;
"paged" = fused page-table output on both sides; us per call):

| GPU | SGLang paged, Gaussian | walk-first paged | SGLang paged, ReLU rows | walk-first paged | 64K full rows: SGLang / walk-first / cutlass_primitives |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B200 | 3.77 | 3.31 | 5.73 | 3.62 | 13.9 / 7.6 / 7.9 |
| H100 PCIe | 3.99 | 3.44 | 6.20 | 3.78 | 14.8 / 8.8 / 8.8 |
| A100 40GB | 4.88 | 4.37 | 7.77 | 5.65 | 19.2 / 11.1 / 11.0 |
| L40S | 3.00 | 2.83 | 4.66 | 3.59 | 11.8 / 7.8 / 7.7 |
| RTX 5080 | 2.61 | 2.42 | 3.98 | 2.64 | 10.0 / 8.1 / 5.7 |
| Rubin (208-SM part) | 3.02 | 2.69 | 4.48 | 2.90 | 12.6 / 6.3 / 5.3 |

Fixed Gaussian rows of 600 to 16K columns run 1.10x to 1.24x faster than SGLang's kernel on
every GPU above; at 256K columns and K 2048 on B200, 49.0 us (SGLang) vs 12.2 us (walk-first).
The existing `gvr_2` backend, measured on the same trace and GPU in the study that motivated
this work, sits at 4.41 us unpaged where `walkfirst_primitives` now takes 3.21 us; that
comparison comes from two sessions, the SGLang columns above from one job each.

End to end in SGLang with the fused decode call taken over and prefill left on SGLang's kernel
(dummy weights, fp8, CUDA graphs): DeepSeek-V4-Flash on one B200, 96 prompts of 1K to 16K
tokens at 16 concurrent, 183.7 / 184.6 output tok/s for walk-first vs 183.6 / 182.1 for
sgl-kernel (median inter-token latency 10.67 vs 10.63 ms); DeepSeek-V3.2 on 8x B200 TP8 (61
indexer layers, K 2048, full-width rows), 80.8 / 81.9 vs 79.7 / 82.5 output tok/s and a decode
step at bs 16 x 32K context of 9.85 vs 10.17 ms. Parity within run-to-run noise with no
regression: the top-k is 1 to 3 percent of a decode step on these models, so the operator-level
wins cannot become a step-time win there.

## 🔍 Related Issues

- #4811 (the `gvr_2` backend this work started from) and #5311 (page-table fusion for `gvr_2`):
  the paged contract here is the same `slot = page_table[q, c // page_size] * page_size + c %
  page_size` mapping, so the two can share tests.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete.

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).
- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

> If you are unsure about how to set up `pre-commit`, see [the pre-commit documentation](https://pre-commit.com/).

## 🧪 Tests

- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.
- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

`tests/topk_varlen/` (801 tests) passes on every architecture: B200 766 passed / 34 skipped /
1 xfailed, Rubin 767 / 33 / 1, RTX 5080 497 / 304, H100 486 / 315, L40S 486 / 315, A100 486 /
315 (the skips are the Blackwell-only `radix`, `gvr`, `gvr_2` and `radix_filter` tests); the
radix_primitives and walk-first suites gate on each backend's own support predicate, so the
Ampere (warp-aggregated collect, register tie fold) and Hopper (no-PDL) variants run there too.
The adversarial exactness sweeps (tie plateaus, one-bin floods, signed zeros, NaN payloads of
either sign, inf floods, rows of every arm) report zero failures on all six.
Value checks compare sorted value multisets, never index sets, so ties cannot make them flaky.
Coverage includes the grouped-row ABI at non-divisible `next_n` x `compress_ratio` boundaries
for every backend that serves it, NaN payloads of either sign per arm, inf floods, tie plateaus
and one-bin floods, top_k above the row width, empty batches, fp16/bf16 on every walk-first arm,
CUDA-graph replay across arm boundaries in both directions, the paged contract (tables wider and
narrower than the width, rows past the coverage, alignment and int32 bounds), one launch per
call, and the input-validation contract. `tests/trace/` passes (1542 passed, 254 skipped).

## 🔬 Experimental Track

<!-- Only for PRs submitted under the experimental policy (CONTRIBUTING.md → "Experimental APIs and Backends").
     Leave this section untouched for normal PRs. -->

- [ ] This PR is **experimental**: it adds or changes code under `flashinfer/experimental/` and/or an `@flashinfer_experimental_api`. Tracking issue: #
  - [ ] The tracking issue names an owner, the reason for the experimental path, and a graduation plan with a target release.
  - [ ] Core changes are limited to a thin entry point (signature, shared validation, feature-gate check, backend selection, handoff).
  - [ ] Tests live in `tests/experimental/` and were validated on the intended hardware; a runnable example is included.
  - [ ] Nothing is registered in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and no experimental backend is reachable from `backend="auto"` without `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`. (Calling an `@flashinfer_experimental_api` or naming a backend explicitly is itself the opt-in and needs no environment variable.)
  - [ ] **Test scope declared below.** The experimental CI lane runs exactly these targets, so keep them as narrow as the change allows.

<!-- Required for experimental PRs. Replace the commented lines below with your targets.
     Do not delete the fence or change its `experimental-tests` tag — the experimental-track
     watcher reads it verbatim to decide which targets to ask CI for. -->

```experimental-tests

# supported -- the sharding runner cannot consume one.) Must be under

```

## Reviewer Notes

Where to start: `flashinfer/topk_varlen/topk_varlen.py` (the checkers, the shared validation,
the paged contract and the `_run_*` dispatchers), then `tests/topk_varlen/test_topk_varlen_paged.py`
for the paged contract, then the kernels in the order of the commits. All four backends are
durable (not experimental): public backend values, two of them auto-routed for paged calls,
all JIT-only (CuTe-DSL kernels and a single-architecture nvcc module are not AOT-compiled, so
`flashinfer/aot.py` is untouched).

Known limitations and intentional deviations:

- **Tie floods are exact, and that costs time where SGLang truncates.** On a 16K-column row
  whose rank-k bin holds thousands of distinct values, SGLang's kernel returns an approximate
  set in 7 to 9 us; walk-first stays exact at 13.6 us on B200 (18 to 27 us on A100). ReLU'd
  indexer logits tie at exact zeros, which the uniform-tie shortcut handles at full speed.
- **Rows just above the 16K short-row cap** take the multi-CTA pipeline, whose fixed floor
  leaves them at 0.83x to 0.94x of SGLang's kernel standalone (the one negative cell in the
  DeepSeek-V3.2 end-to-end run, bs 16 at 16K context, 9.81 vs 9.62 ms per step).
- **Ampere/Ada compile a register fold of the tie key range** (cc 8.x serialise same-address
  shared-memory reductions): plateaus 2.2x to 3.4x faster and ReLU rows 21 to 25 percent faster
  there, Gaussian rows about 5 percent (0.1 to 0.2 us) slower. SM90+ compile the direct form.
- **`radix_primitives` waits for the producer before its first global read** (PDL on SM90+;
  the lengths and the page table may come from the preceding kernel, so the earlier metadata
  prefetch was a race). Same-node A/B against the pre-review kernel (B200, two alternating
  rounds, `cutlass_primitives` as the unchanged control column): ReLU paged rows 3.69 to
  3.83 us, 2048-column rows 3.85 to 4.05 us, 16K rows 6.10 to 6.30 us; Gaussian paged rows,
  full rows and every A100 cell unchanged. Walk-first already waited first and is unchanged.
- **Prefill is not taken over.** The kernels are 1.0x to 1.9x faster than SGLang's at prefill
  shapes, but the API specialises a kernel per logits width and prefill chunks present many
  widths; an engine must pad to a fixed width before using these backends there.
- **NaN order.** fp32 ranks every NaN top like `torch.topk` in all three primitives kernels. For
  fp16/bf16 the short-row arms and `radix_primitives` bin the integer key, so a sign-set NaN
  pattern ranks bottom there (top in walk-first's long-row pipeline); documented in the kernel
  docstrings, and real logits do not carry negative NaNs.
- **`sglang` keeps upstream's PDL prefetch**: on SM90+ it reads `seq_lens` and the page-table
  row before its grid-dependency wait, so under programmatic dependent launch the kernel
  immediately preceding the call must not write them (the backend docstring states this; the
  primitives kernels wait before their first global read). It is kept as the kernel SGLang
  runs so the parity and API-overhead checks (API 3.32 us vs raw kernel 3.35 us on the decode
  trace) stay reproducible.
- **`approx_ties`** is honoured by `radix_primitives` only (the docstring says so); `sglang` is
  approximate regardless; exact backends ignore it.
- **`workspace["cutlass_primitives_row_order"]`** hands the caller a CTA-scheduling decision
  (longest rows first pairs long rows against short ones: up to 17 percent on skewed batches).
  An in-call ranking launch measured 1.3 us and loses on uniform batches, so the backend never
  computes it itself; the key is validated (shape, dtype, device) but its contents are trusted.
  Happy to drop the key if the maintainers prefer the API without a scheduling knob.
- **Vendored code:** `flashinfer/topk_varlen/cutlass_primitives/` is an unmodified vendoring
  (edit upstream and re-vendor; comment style and `docs/` references follow the upstream
  library). Three upstream-side items found in review are left for the library: the cluster
  verdict's re-published words have no cluster barrier between a peer's first-round reads and
  the second round (unreachable in practice: the window is a whole filter pass), `_scaled_rank`
  can overflow int32 above a 131072-element aim on 99 KB parts (exact result, perf cliff), and
  `max_active_clusters` falls back silently when the occupancy probe fails.
  `csrc/sglang_dsv4/sgl_kernel/` is verbatim upstream sglang and excluded from the formatting
  hooks so it stays diffable; its launcher documents that the raw ragged entry does not clamp
  lengths to the row width (the `top_k_varlen` entry does, on device).
- **Auto routing:** the primitives backends are outside the unpaged `auto` ranking and are
  selected by `auto` only when a page table is given, where the two exact ones are the only
  candidates.

Pre-submission review: the diff was walked against `docs/code_review_guidance.md` by seven
dimension reviewers each followed by an adversarial verifier (about eighty confirmed findings
from crash risks to nits; every bug and test gap was fixed before opening, the remaining items
are the deviations listed above). One more nit left as is: walk-first's cluster retry
re-publishes two shared words without a cluster barrier between the peers' first-round DSMEM
reads and the overwrite; the reads are issued at the barrier and the overwrite follows a full
re-walk, so the window is not reachable on hardware. The fixes cover the vendored sglang module
building for exactly one architecture per device capability (its headers static-assert the
target against the global gencode list), the paged `sglang` path clamping to a narrow table as
the API promises, device and alignment checks in its launcher, checkers that encode every

compile keys, a capture-safe cluster-capacity probe, the shared validation of `seq_lens`'
device, `top_k` and `compress_ratio`, and license and provenance files for both vendored trees.

📌 Description
This PR updates the Hopper CUTLASS grouped MoE backend for mixed low-precision
inputs. It improves the existing Hopper W4 grouped GEMM paths and adds a new
MXFP4 weight + FP8 activation path:
MXFP4xBF16: optimize the existing MXFP4 weight + BF16 activation path.
INT4xFP8: optimize the existing INT4 weight + FP8 activation path.
MXFP4xFP8: add MXFP4 weight + FP8 activation with pre-MMA E8M0 scale fusion and runtime
per-token FP8 activation quantization.
The MXFP4xFP8 path follows the high-level weight preprocessing and
dequantization idea used by
Humming
:
the MXFP4 weight scale is transformed into a bounded E8M0 exponent offset and
folded into the FP8 operand before MMA. FlashInfer keeps this flow integrated
with its fused MoE runtime, autotune, and CUTLASS extension backend.
The implementation keeps the changes inside FlashInfer's CUTLASS extension
layer rather than modifying vendored CUTLASS. The main changes are:
Enable Hopper FP4 kernels without requiring CUDA native FP4 headers on SM90
by using CUTLASS subbyte FP4 types.
Add optimized mixed-input mainloops for post-MMA scaling and pre-MMA E8M0
scale fusion.
Precompute grouped GEMM work scheduling and TMA descriptor state before the
main GEMM kernel.
Use folded weight-scale storage so the weight-scale layout is independent of
the profiled
TileK
.
Add precomputed scheduler kernels for ping-pong and cooperative grouped GEMM
schedulers.
Add runtime activation expansion and per-token FP8 quantization support for
the pre-MMA E8M0 scale-fusion path.
Add per-token scale epilogue callbacks for the FP8 activation + MXFP4 weight
path.
Extend autotune and tactic validation so Hopper mixed-input tactics are
checked for correctness before being selected.
Add and update tests for Hopper MXFP4xBF16, INT4xFP8, and MXFP4xFP8 pre-MMA scale
paths.
🔍 Related Issues
N/A
Performance
Benchmarks were run on NVIDIA H20 and H200 GPUs using MoE workload configurations matching DeepSeek-V3 (256 experts, top-8, hidden size 7168, intermediate size 2048) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (384 experts, top-6, hidden size 7168, intermediate size 3072).
https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3
https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro
The plots below summarize the PR performance results. Raw benchmark tables are intentionally not embedded in this PR text.
INT4xFP8 and MXFP4xBF16 vs Same-Path Baseline
The existing INT4xFP8 and MXFP4xBF16 paths generally improve over the same-path
baseline after the Hopper mixed-input backend changes.
|
Current fused MoE speedup vs same-path baseline
Current Paths vs Current FP8 Per-Tensor Baseline
This compares the current fused MoE mixed-input paths against the current FP8
per-tensor path.
|
Current fused MoE path speedup vs current FP8 per-tensor
MXFP4xFP8 Pre-MMA Scale Path vs Upstream Humming (2026/06/23 commit f6241bb)
The pre-MMA E8M0 scale-fusion path is compared against upstream Humming GEMM
timings. Positive values mean FlashInfer is faster.
|
DS4 FlashInfer Humming GEMM speedup vs upstream Humming
Implementation Notes
The Hopper FP4 compatibility path uses CUTLASS FP4 storage on SM90 and keeps
CUDA native FP4 as a toolkit-dependent feature instead of a Hopper
requirement.
The mixed-input grouped GEMM scheduler now supports a precomputed work map.
This avoids doing grouped tile lookup and descriptor updates in the main GEMM
hot path.
The folded weight-scale layout decouples model preprocessing from the
selected
TileK
, which lets autotune choose among multiple
TileK
values
without requiring multiple prepacked weight-scale layouts.
The pre-MMA E8M0 scale path fuses the weight scale into FP8 operands before
WGMMA and applies the activation token scale in the epilogue.
The MXFP4xFP8 pre-MMA scale path is inspired by Humming's weight
preprocessing/dequantization flow:
https://github.com/inclusionAI/humming
The runtime FP8 activation quantization path computes per-token activation
scales while expanding routed MoE rows.
The autotune validation path now rejects tactics that fail correctness before
timing and selection.
